abstract: Pollination in apple (Malus domestica Borkh.) is typically attributed to diurnal bees, yet nocturnal insects also contribute to fruit set. To assess whether apple flowers recruit potential pollinators throughout the 24-hour cycle, we quantified diel patterns in floral attractants and insect visitation in an orchard in Northwest Arkansas, United States. We measured nectar and volatiles and used a combination of visual surveys, light traps, and video recordings to assess insect abundance and floral visitation while controlling for weather conditions. We found that nectar volume remained consistent across sampling times, indicating that reward availability is dielly stable. Floral volatile bouquets, in contrast, exhibited subtle but significant diel and interannual variation, driven largely by shifts in aldehydes, alkanes, and benzenoids. Several compounds associated with nocturnal moth and dipteran attraction - including alpha-farnesene, benzyl alcohol, and aldehydes - were enriched at night. Apple flowers were visited by insects around the clock. Nighttime visitors were less abundant than daytime visitors but taxonomically diverse, including moths and nematoceran flies, whereas bees, wasps, and brachyceran flies were restricted to daytime. Different taxonomic groups therefore alternated over the diel cycle, producing pronounced shifts in visitor community composition. Thus, apple flowers produce attractants across the diel cycle and nocturnal insects - particularly dipterans and moths - are a consistent, ecologically meaningful component of the apple flower-visiting assemblage. Our findings support the need for pollinator-inclusive management that accounts for the full diel cycle, particularly when scheduling pesticide applications near bloom, to sustain diverse pollinator communities and enhance the resilience of apple production systems.
